newsitem.title: USA: Agouron, Vertex in drug race.
newsitem.headline: Agouron, Vertex in drug race.

text.p: Rival biotechnology companies Agouron Pharmaceuticals Inc and Vertex Pharmaceuticals Inc said separately on Friday they had identifed a protein key to replication of the hepatitis C virus.

They both indicated they would use their information in a race to come up with a drug to treat the malady, which causes chronic liver inflammation and is estimated to affect about two percent of the U.S. population.
Analysts said such a drug could be a huge seller, with potential annual sales in the U.S. alone of at least $500 million. But a drug is likely years from reaching the market.
"I think it's a dead heat," said Montgomery Securities analyst Scott Sacane of the hepatitis C drug race between Agouron and Vertex.

"From a standing start, if they get to human clinical trials within three years, they'd be doing very well," he said. Getting to final U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval of a drug could take another four years, he said.
Dueling scientific papers on the structure of the hepatitis C protease enzyme were published on Friday in the scientific journal Cell.

There is no vaccine available to prevent hepatitis C infection. The only drug approved for the treatment of hepatitis C, interferon alpha, provides long-term benefit to only about 25 percent of patients treated, according to Vertex.

The findings are the latest in a string of discoveries of viral protease enzymes, including those involved in the reproduction of HIV, herpes and rhinovirus, the most frequent cause of the common cold.
HIV protease inhibitors, used in combination with older-line therapies such as AZT, have driven the virus that causes AIDS to undetectable levels in infected patients.
Several drug companies, including Merck and Co Inc, Abbott Laboratories Inc, Agouron and Vertex, have developed HIV protease inhibitor drugs.
